message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the most important tenant‑rights provisions under Texas law. These rights apply to most residential leases (apartments, single‑family homes, etc.) and are enforced by the Texas Attorney General’s Office, local housing agencies, and the courts. | Area | What You’re Entitled To | Key Points | |------|------------------------|------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out (unless you and the landlord agree otherwise).
• Landlord may keep a deposit only for:
 – Unpaid rent
 – Damage beyond normal wear & tear
 – Cleaning costs if the unit isn’t left in a reasonable condition | • Landlord must provide a written itemized statement of deductions.
• If the landlord fails to return the deposit, you can sue for the full amount plus damages. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• You can withhold rent or repair and deduct if the landlord fails to act within a reasonable time. | • Texas law requires the landlord to fix major problems within **30 days** of notice.
• For minor repairs, the landlord must respond within **5 days**. | | **Notice of Entry** | • Landlord must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** before entering, except in emergencies. | • Entry is allowed for inspections, repairs, or showing the unit to prospective tenants. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but the increase must be **reasonable** and not discriminatory. | • For lease renewals, the landlord can set a new rate; for month‑to‑month, they can raise rent with proper notice (usually 30 days). | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • The Fair Housing Act applies to all residential rentals in Texas. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term lease**: Landlord must provide a valid reason (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease) and follow the lease’s termination clause. | • If you break the lease early, you may be liable for rent until the unit is re‑rented, unless the landlord can prove they found a new tenant quickly. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **notice** (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an eviction lawsuit. | • Texas courts will enforce the eviction only after a judgment is entered. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • You have the right to “quiet enjoyment” of the property. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise specified in the lease. | • If utilities are not provided, you may be able to pay for them yourself and deduct from rent. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlord must keep common areas (hallways, elevators, laundry rooms) clean and safe. | • If common areas are unsafe, you can request repairs or withhold rent. | | **Right to Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem within a reasonable time, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent. | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, local housing agency, or the court.
• Small claims court can award up to $10,000 for damages. | • Document all communication and keep copies of the lease, notices, and repair requests. | --- #### Practical Steps to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Note any clauses about repairs, deposits, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, and written records of any problems or landlord interactions. 3. **Give Written Notice** – When reporting issues, send a copy via certified mail or email with a read receipt. 4. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law sets specific time frames for repairs and entry; keep track of deadlines. 5. **Seek Legal Help if Needed** – If a landlord violates your rights, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid organization. --- #### Quick Reference: How to File a Complaint | Agency | Contact | What to Provide | |--------|---------|-----------------| | Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division | 1‑800‑252‑6420 or online form | Lease, photos, correspondence, proof of payment | | Local Housing Agency (e.g., city or county) | Check city website | Same as above | | Small Claims Court | County courthouse | Lease, receipts, evidence of damages | --- **Disclaimer:** This overview is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may affect your rights. If you’re facing a dispute, consider consulting a qualified attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
